note: set under NOTÆ in two columns (Greek lemma then Latin comment, across both columns); marker printed as bracketed letter '(e)'; first half of the note is on this page, rest on p-0310

anchorLine: Neque haec est pars Jacob, ait qui dixit k; sed

text: [continuation of note (e) from p-0309, under NOTÆ] dissiparentur et diffluerent; hincque rerum generationes et excidia forent, quod praeter corpora et inanitatem Epicurus aliud nihil in mundo agnosceret. Qua de re epistola ejus prima ad Herodotum. Sic velit Maximus Severianorum errore sequi, factam Incarnationem non destinata Verbi voluntate assumente naturam humanam, sibique uniente, sed fortuito quasi, vel naturarum (vel magis qualitatum) concursu, quo praeter casum, etiam Manetis ac reliquorum veterum haereticorum δόκησις et phantasma, seu inane spectrum, inducitur.
en: [Continuation of (e)] ... would be scattered and flow apart; and hence the generations and destructions of things would occur, since Epicurus recognised nothing else in the world besides bodies and the void. On this matter see his first letter to Herodotus. Thus Maximus would seem to follow the error of the Severians: the Incarnation having come about not by the Word's appointed will, assuming and uniting to himself human nature, but as if by chance, or by a concourse of natures (or rather of qualities), by which, besides chance, the 'appearance' (dokesis) and phantasm of Manes and the other ancient heretics, that is, an empty ghost, is introduced.
note: continuation; anchor is on p-0309 (see marker e there). Spelling in the print: 'hæreticorum', 'præter', 'Verbi'; transcribed with ae for æ
